metadata.title: FINANCIAL AND CREDIT ACTIVITY: PROBLEMS OF THEORY AND PRACTICE
metadata.venue: ФІНАНСОВО-КРЕДИТНА ДІЯЛЬНІСТЬ: ПРОБЛЕМИ ТЕОРІЇ ТА ПРАКТИКИ

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses country-level PISA performance indicators (average scores across mathematics, reading, and science) rather than student-level microdata. Because the analysis is conducted on aggregated country outcomes and external macro indicators (e.g., HDI, GDP PPP, R&D shares), the paper does not report the use of PISA sampling/survey weights (e.g., student weights such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures. The methodology section describes regression/correlation modeling and curve fitting, not complex-survey estimation. Therefore, any weighting that would normally be applied to PISA microdata is not applicable in the reported design; the results should be interpreted as relationships among country averages and system-level indicators.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the reported analyses are country-level average PISA scores (and system-level indicators like HDI and GDP PPP), not PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes at the student level. As a result, Plausible Values handling is not applicable to the reported modeling. The paper also does not describe any missing-data procedure for the constructed country-level dataset (e.g., how missing macro indicators or PISA-derived averages were handled), which is a reporting gap for transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper constructs a country-level dataset using PISA results for 2015, 2018, and 2022 (average scores across mathematics, reading, and science) and links them to cumulative 9-year education expenditures per 15/16-year-old student (USD at PPP). For the long-term modeling, countries are split into two groups based on R&D expenditure (% of GDP): low R&D (up to 0.9% of GDP) and high R&D (0.9–5.6% of GDP). The paper further identifies leading and lagging countries using PISA 2022 outcomes relative to the standard deviation limits around an approximating quadratic model, producing a shortlist of countries with outcomes outside the standard error range. No student-level inclusion/exclusion criteria, grade restrictions, or microdata filtering steps are described because the analysis is performed on aggregated country indicators.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 outcomes relative to the standard deviati the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This article evaluates the effectiveness of general secondary education financing by relating country-level PISA outcomes to education expenditure measures and broader societal indicators. It uses PISA 2015, PISA 2018, and PISA 2022 average scores across mathematics, reading, and science, and tests curve approximations (including inverse quadratic/polynomial forms) to characterize a non-linear relationship between cumulative 9-year education spending (USD at PPP) and PISA performance. For PISA 2022, it identifies leading and lagging countries (e.g., Vietnam, Singapore, Macao, Japan vs. Qatar, Panama, Cyprus, Dominican Republic, Thailand) based on deviations from the fitted curve beyond standard deviation/standard error limits. For long-term system success, it models HDI as a function of R&D expenditure (% GDP) and per-student educational spending adjusted for PISA scores in the high-R&D group, reporting R² = 69.7% and a significant Fisher test. Limitations include the absence of student-level PV handling, no reported missing-data strategy, and no ML model comparison/validation framework because the analysis is primarily regression/correlation and curve fitting on aggregated indicators. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: This article evaluates the effectiveness of general secondary education financing by relating country-level PISA outcomes to education expenditure measures and broader societal indicators. For long-term system success, it models HDI as a function of R&D expenditure (% GDP) and per-student educational spending adjusted for PISA scores in the high-R&D group, reporting R² = 69.7% and a significant Fisher test. data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the paper is empirical and uses PISA-derived outcomes, it does not implement machine learning algorithms for predictive modeling, nor does it report PV handling or missing-data procedures at the student level. The extraction therefore leaves ml_techniques empty and main_findings empty because the schema requires StructuredFinding rows only for distinct ML target variables with ML performance metrics. The study’s quantitative results are presented as curve fits and linear regression statistics on country-level aggregates rather than ML prediction tasks.
